content: ILF3, also known as Interleukin Enhancer-Binding Factor 3, is a protein encoded by the ILF3 gene in humans. The nuclear factor of activated T-cells (NFAT) is a transcription factor that is essential for the expression of interleukin-2 (IL-2) in T-cells. NFAT binds to a specific sequence within the IL-2 enhancer, referred to as the antigen receptor response element 2. Beyond its role in transcriptional regulation, NFAT also has the ability to bind RNA and plays a critical role in the encapsidation and protein priming of the hepatitis B viral polymerase. Structurally, NFAT is a heterodimer composed of two proteins with molecular weights of 45 kDa and 90 kDa, the latter of which is the product of the ILF3 gene. The ILF3-encoded protein is predominantly localized to ribosomes and is believed to regulate transcription at the level of mRNA elongation. At least three transcript variants encoding distinct isoforms of this protein have been identified. ILF3 has been shown to interact with several proteins and molecules, including DNA-PKcs, FUS, PRMT1, protein kinase R, and XPO5. Additionally, ILF3 interacts with small NF90/ILF3-associated RNAs (snaRs), which are approximately 120 nucleotides in length and contain double-stranded RNA-binding motifs. One such RNA, snaR-A, is highly abundant in human testes and has been observed to associate with ribosomes in HeLa cells. Interestingly, snaR-A is present in humans and gorillas but is absent in chimpanzees. Other snaR RNAs have been identified in African great apes, including chimpanzees and bonobos. Both ILF2 and ILF3 have been identified as autoantigens in various autoimmune conditions. These include induced lupus in mice, systemic rheumatic autoimmune disease in dogs, and, albeit rarely, autoimmune diseases in humans.
